Prosperity
prŏs-pĕr´ĭ-tĭ
n. (success, flourishing; rendering Hebrew shalvah and tsalach)
From Latin prosperare, to cause to succeed. Scripture treats prosperity as a real blessing and a serious hazard, often in the same passage.

Biblical Definition

Prosperity is flourishing. Ecclesiastes sets it opposite adversity as equally appointed: “In the day of prosperity be joyful, but in the day of adversity consider” (Ecc 7:14). The psalmist confesses envying the prosperity of the wicked until he went into the sanctuary (Psa 73:3,17). Solomon's own dedication asks for wisdom rather than riches, and prosperity followed unasked (1Ki 3:11–13); and David warns, “in my prosperity I said, I shall never be moved” (Psa 30:6).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines prosperity as advance or gain in any thing good or desirable; successful progress in any business or enterprise; success; attainment of the object desired.

PROSPERITY, n. Advance or gain in any thing good or desirable; successful progress in any business or enterprise; success; attainment of the object desired.

Key Scripture

Ecc 7:14 — "In the day of prosperity be joyful, but in the day of adversity consider: God also hath set the one over against the other, to the end that man should find nothing after him."

Psa 73:3 — "For I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked."

Psa 30:6 — "And in my prosperity I said, I shall never be moved."

Psa 73:17 — "Until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end."

Modern Corruption

Prosperity is read as proof of God's approval, and Psalm 73 records a believer nearly losing his footing over how well the wicked were doing.

expand to see more

Psalm 73 is the most honest chapter in Scripture about envy. My feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped. For I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked. The psalmist catalogues their ease, their health, their freedom from trouble, and admits the conclusion he drew: verily I have cleansed my heart in vain. What changed was not his circumstances but his vantage point — until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end.

David's line in Psalm 30:6 is the shortest diagnosis of prosperity's hazard: in my prosperity I said, I shall never be moved. Nothing sinful is described. The danger is a sentence a comfortable man says to himself, and the next verse records what it took to correct it: thou didst hide thy face, and I was troubled.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shalvah (H7962), ease, prosperity; tsalach (H6743), to prosper or succeed; shalom (H7965), peace, welfare.

expand to see more

Hebrew shalvah (H7962) — ease, prosperity; Psalm 73:3, Proverbs 1:32, the prosperity of fools shall destroy them.

Hebrew tsalach (H6743) — to prosper; Genesis 39:2, Joshua 1:8, Psalm 1:3.

Hebrew tob (H2896) — good; Ecclesiastes 7:14, the day of prosperity.

Usage

"“I was envious… when I saw the prosperity of the wicked” — a believer nearly slipping."

"“Until I went into the sanctuary of God” — the vantage point that changed."

"“In my prosperity I said, I shall never be moved” — the sentence comfort teaches."
